claim: Striatal cholinergic interneurons (CINs) are key modulators of the striatal microcircuitry, impacting neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity of spiny projection neurons (SPNs), as well as other striatal interneurons.
source: The striatal cholinergic interneuron (CIN) is a key modulator of the striatal microcircuitry, impacting the neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity of spiny projection neurons (SPNs), as well as other striatal interneurons (Abudukeyoumu et al., 2019; Assous, 2021; Goldberg et al., 2012; Matityahu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Two glutamatergic inputs arising from cerebral cortex and intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus can drive CINs to discharge.
source: First, the two glutamatergic inputs arising from cerebral cortex and intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus can drive CINs to discharge (Bradfield et al., 2013; Ding et al., 2010; Doig et al., 2014; Kosillo et al., 2016; Lapper and Bolam, 1992; Mamaligas et al., 2019; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Sharott et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The unitary synaptic currents generated by cortical and thalamic inputs in CINs are identical.
source: While the unitary synaptic currents generated by these two inputs in CINs are identical (Aceves Buendia et al., 2019), thalamic inputs to CINs dominate in the sense that they that give rise to larger excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) in acute striatal slices (Johansson and Silberberg, 2020) and can trigger abrupt pause responses, often flanked by excitatory peaks, to external saliency-related cues (Apicella et al., 1991; Goldberg and Reynolds, 2011; Graybiel et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Thalamic inputs to CINs give rise to larger excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) in acute striatal slices than cortical inputs.
source: While the unitary synaptic currents generated by these two inputs in CINs are identical (Aceves Buendia et al., 2019), thalamic inputs to CINs dominate in the sense that they that give rise to larger excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) in acute striatal slices (Johansson and Silberberg, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Thalamic inputs can trigger abrupt pause responses in CINs, often flanked by excitatory peaks, to external saliency-related cues.
source: thalamic inputs to CINs dominate in the sense that they that give rise to larger excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) in acute striatal slices (Johansson and Silberberg, 2020) and can trigger abrupt pause responses, often flanked by excitatory peaks, to external saliency-related cues (Apicella et al., 1991; Goldberg and Reynolds, 2011; Graybiel et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical inputs to CINs give rise to smaller EPSPs in most CINs in acute striatal slices.
source: In contrast, cortical inputs to CINs are weaker in that, in acute striatal slices, they give rise to smaller EPSPs in most CINs (Mamaligas et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cortical inputs to CINs cannot trigger the pause response in acute striatal slices.
source: In contrast, cortical inputs to CINs are weaker in that, in acute striatal slices, they give rise to smaller EPSPs in most CINs (Mamaligas et al., 2019) and cannot trigger the pause response (Ding et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The differences between cortical and thalamic inputs to CINs are less pronounced in intact animals.
source: although, these differences are less pronounced in intact animals (Doig et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CINs exhibit multiple autonomously generated discharge patterns including regular and irregular pacemaking, as well as burst firing.
source: Second, even in the absence of afferent input, CINs exhibit multiple autonomously generated discharge patterns – including regular and irregular pacemaking, as well as burst firing (Bennett et al., 2000; Bennett and Wilson, 1999; Goldberg and Reynolds, 2011; Goldberg and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CIN firing patterns are generated by an interplay between various nonlinear ionic currents including voltage- and Ca2+-activated K+ currents, as well as two voltage-dependent pacemaker currents: the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) current and the persistent Na+ (NaP) current.
source: These firing patterns are generated by an interplay between various nonlinear ionic currents including voltage- and Ca2+-activated K+ currents, as well as two voltage-dependent pacemaker currents: the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) current; and the persistent Na+ (NaP) current (Bennett et al., 2000; Deng et al., 2007; Goldberg et al., 2009; Goldberg and Wilson, 2010; Goldberg and Wilson, 2005; McGuirt et al., 2021; Oswald et al., 2009; Song and Surmeier, 1996; Wilson, 2005; Wilson and Goldberg, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The HCN current is mostly active below –60 mV and is responsible for the voltage sag in response to a hyperpolarizing current pulse.
source: The HCN current is mostly active below –60 mV and is responsible for the voltage sag in response to a hyperpolarizing current pulse (Figure 1A, 'HCN')
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the voltage sag.

claim: The NaP current takes over at –60 mV and is necessary and sufficient to drive CINs to action potential threshold.
source: whereas the NaP current takes over at –60 mV and is necessary and sufficient (Bennett et al., 2000) to drive CINs to action potential threshold (Figure 1A, 'NaP').
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: When CINs were held at –55 mV, the impedance curve exhibited an amplifying structure, with the phase delay being strictly positive.
source: As expected (Figure 1C, black), the impedance curve, |Z(f)|, exhibited an amplifying structure, with the phase delay being strictly positive.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The amplifying parameter µn was estimated to be –3.9 when CINs were held at –55 mV.
source: In this fit, there is a (negative) amplifying parameter, µn – that is derived from biophysical properties of amplifying current (e.g. the slope of the activation curve, reversal potential, etc.) (Goldberg et al., 2007) – which was estimated to be µn = –3.9.
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: When neurons were held at –70 mV, the impedance revealed a clear resonance peak at approximately 1 Hz, and a zero crossing at a slightly lower frequency.
source: Estimation of the amplitude response and phase delay (Figure 1C, red), revealed significantly different curves (amplitude: p=6·10–25, phase: p=1·10–17, ANCOVA) with a clear resonance peak at approximately 1 Hz, and a zero crossing at a slightly lower frequency (Figure 1C, red).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: At –70 mV holding potential, the amplifying parameter was estimated to be µn = –3.4 and the resonance parameter was estimated to be µh=1.6.
source: Fitting the somatic phase delay yielded a reasonable fit only when both an amplifying and resonant component were included in the fit with the amplifying parameter (µn = –3.4) being only slightly reduced relative to the –55 mV fit. In contrast, the additional (positive) resonance parameter, µh – which is derived from the biophysical properties of the restorative current – was estimated to be µh=1.6
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Application of 1 µM TTX reduced the impedance and exhibited a trend toward a shortened phase delay.
source: This conclusion was supported by the fact that application of 1 µM TTX (n=9 neurons, N=4 mice), that abolished autonomous spiking and slightly hyperpolarized the CIN (Figure 2A), reduced the impedance (p=9·10–9) and exhibited a trend toward a shortened phase delay (P=0.137, ANCOVA, Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: Application of 10 µM ZD7288 abolished the sag response.
source: Similarly, application of 10 µM ZD7288, the selective HCN antagonist (n=9 neurons, N=7 mice), which abolished the sag response (Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Application of 10 µM ZD7288 abolished the resonance peak in the impedance curve and significantly reduced the negative lobe in the phase delay.
source: application of 10 µM ZD7288, the selective HCN antagonist (n=9 neurons, N=7 mice), which abolished the sag response (Figure 2C), abolished the resonance peak in the impedance curve (p=4·10–16) and significantly reduced the negative lobe in the phase delay (p=0.018, ANCOVA, Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: ZD7288 reduced the resonance parameter to µh=0.5.
source: which was captured by the resonance parameter being reduced to µh=0.5.
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Comparison of the somatic current traces in response to proximal vs. full-field illumination demonstrated that the phase of the full-field-generated current is delayed relative to the proximally-generated current.
source: Comparison of the somatic current traces in response to proximal (Figure 3B, black) vs. full-field (red) illumination demonstrated that the phase of the full-field-generated current is delayed relative to the proximally-generated current.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At –55 mV holding potential, the full-field illumination activated roughly twice the electrotonic range (r=1.07) that was activated by the proximal illumination (r=0.46).
source: We found that fitting our model of ChR2 kinetics to the significantly-different phases observed in the proximal and full-field illuminations at –55 mV (n=5 neurons, N=4 mice, p=4·10–3, ANCOVA) yielded that the full-field illumination activated roughly twice the electrotonic range (r=1.07) that was activated by the proximal illumination (r=0.46, Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At –70 mV holding potential, the phase delays at the lower frequencies (especially at 0.4 Hz) were negative.
source: In this case (n=14 neurons, N=10 mice), the phase delays at the lower frequencies (especially at 0.4 Hz) were negative, which was reminiscent of the results from the electrical voltage stimulation experiments (Figure 1) at the –70 mV holding potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At –70 mV, the restorative parameter was estimated to be larger for the proximal fit (µh=3.4) relative to the full field fit (µh=1.7).
source: Here too the restorative parameter was estimated to be larger for the proximal fit (µh=3.4) relative to the full field fit (µh=1.7), suggesting that the HCN currents are denser more proximally.
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data and inference about HCN current distribution.

claim: The negative phase delays in the subhertz frequency range tended to be less negative for the full-field illumination.
source: The conclusion that the HCN current is concentrated proximally is buttressed by the fact that the negative phase delays in the subhertz frequency range tended to be less negative for the full-field illumination (P=0.037, Wilcoxon rank-sum test on phase delays at 0.4 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: TTX application increased the somatic current's amplitude response for full-field illumination.
source: While full-field illumination in TTX increased the somatic current's amplitude response (control: n=9 neurons, N=7 mice; TTX: n=14 neurons, N=8 mice, p=7·10–9, ANCOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis.

claim: TTX application reduced the somatic current's amplitude response for proximal illumination.
source: proximal illumination in TTX reduced the somatic current's amplitude response (control: n=9 neurons, N=7 mice; TTX: n=12 neurons, N=6 mice, p=1.1·10–4, ANCOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis.

claim: The pharmacological result provides model-independent evidence that the NaP currents are expressed primarily proximally and less so distally.
source: Thus, this pharmacological result provides model-independent evidence that the NaP currents are expressed primarily proximally and less so distally.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of TTX on proximal vs. full-field illumination.

claim: The persistent and fast-inactivating Nav currents flow through the same Nav channels.
source: The persistent and fast-inactivating Nav currents flow through the same Nav channels (Alzheimer et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The size of the bAP-driven Ca2+ transients remains constant up to approximately 70 µm from the soma, and then drops off.
source: Neglecting that effect, we found that the size of the bAP-driven Ca2+ transients remains constant up to approximately 70 µm from the soma, and then drops off.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In 7 CINs where measurements of ∆F/F0 were made at both proximal and distal (>70 µm) locations, the median distal signal was significantly lower than the proximal one by 29%.
source: Additionally, in 7 CINs (N=5 mice) in which we had measurements of ∆F/F0 at both proximal and distal (>70 µm) locations, we found that the median distal signal was significantly lower than the proximal one by 29% (p=0.047, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The spatial dependence of the Ca2+ transient amplitude suggests that the bAP maintains a constant amplitude due to the presence of Nav channels that sustain their regenerative nature out to some 70 µm from the soma.
source: This spatial dependence of the Ca2+ transient amplitude, suggests that the bAP maintains a constant amplitude due to the presence of Nav channels that sustain their regenerative nature out to some 70 µm from the soma.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: Ranolazine failed to reduce the amplitude of monosynaptic corticostriatal EPSPs to CINs in wildtype mice.
source: Interestingly, we found in acute striatal slices from these wildtype mice that ranolazine failed to reduce the amplitude of monosynaptic corticostriatal EPSPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) to CINs (n=11 neurons, N=6 mice, p=0.74, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: Cortical inputs to CINs are not normally boosted in wildtype mice.
source: ranolazine failed to reduce the amplitude of monosynaptic corticostriatal EPSPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) to CINs (n=11 neurons, N=6 mice, p=0.74, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 5B), indicating the cortical inputs to CINs are not normally boosted.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of ranolazine effect on cortical EPSPs.

claim: The mean amplitude of PfN EPSPs was reduced by a median of 16% by ranolazine.
source: Indeed, the mean amplitude of the EPSP was reduced by a median of 16% (n=11 neurons, N=4 mice, p=0.04, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claim: Ranolazine had no effect on paired-pulse ratios at either cortical or PfN synapses.
source: Importantly, ranolazine had no effect on paired-pulse ratios (Aceves Buendia et al., 2019) at either cortical or PfN synapses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), ruling out a presynaptic mechanism-of-action.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claim: The post-synaptic boosting of glutamatergic inputs to CINs by NaP currents occurs in dendritic regions that correspond to the spatial localization of these currents.
source: Thus, we conclude that the post-synaptic boosting of glutamatergic inputs to CINs by NaP currents occurs in dendritic regions that correspond to the spatial localization of these currents as derived from the quasi-linear properties of CINs and from 2PLSM imaging of bAPs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: CINs exhibit a membrane resonance in the subhertz range that depends on the holding potential.
source: As previously reported by Beatty and collaborators (Beatty et al., 2015), CIN somata exhibit a membrane resonance in the subhertz range, that depends on the holding potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research and confirmed by current study data.

claim: SPNs exhibit no resonance.
source: In contrast, SPNs exhibit no resonance (Beatty et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TANs exhibit stronger entrainment to slow-wave LFP events during sleep, while SPNs under the same conditions do not.
source: we hypothesized that the tonically active neurons (TANs) in the NHP striatum – that are comprised primarily of CINs (Aosaki et al., 1995; Kawaguchi, 1993; Wilson et al., 1990) – will exhibit stronger entrainment to slow-wave LFP events during sleep, while SPNs under the same conditions will not.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis that is then tested with experimental data.

claim: While the firing rate of SPNs was unaffected by slow wave events, the firing rates of TANs was modulated by these slow-wave events.
source: Indeed, triggering the spike trains of TANs and SPNs (from N=2 NHPs) on slow wave events that occur during sleep stages N2 and N3 (Mizrahi-Kliger et al., 2018; Riedner et al., 2007), which represent relatively deep non-REM sleep, demonstrates that while the firing rate of SPNs was unaffected (n=83), the firing rates of TANs (n=122) was modulated by these slow-wave events (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-E.

claim: TANs firing was not modulated during higher frequency sleep spindle events.
source: In contrast, the TANs firing was not modulated during higher frequency sleep spindle events (Figure 6F–H), in agreement with the subhertz membrane resonance peak we observed in the acute slice experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: The biphasic response exhibited by TANs to slow-wave events bears a striking resemblance to the 'classical' TAN response to external cues.
source: Importantly, the biphasic response exhibited by TANs to slow-wave events bears a striking resemblance to the 'classical' TAN response to external cues (Aosaki et al., 1995; Apicella et al., 1991; Joshua et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior research cited.

claim: TAN responses to external cues in awake primates require an intact thalamic projection.
source: Because these responses in awake primates require an intact thalamic projection (Bradfield et al., 2013; Goldberg and Reynolds, 2011; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Schulz and Reynolds, 2013; Smith et al., 2004; Yamanaka et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: This is the first report of striatal TANs responding to an internally generated brain event, and not an external saliency-related cue.
source: Importantly, because the primates are asleep in a sound-proof room, this is, to the best of our knowledge, the first report of striatal TANs responding to an internally generated brain event, and not an external saliency-related cue.
evidence: The claim is a novel finding from the current study.

claim: Thalamic inputs terminate perisomatically and on proximal dendrites of CINs.
source: with cortical inputs terminating on distal dendrites and thalamic inputs terminating perisomatically and on proximal dendrites (Doig et al., 2014; Lapper and Bolam, 1992; Mamaligas et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical inputs terminate on distal dendrites of CINs.
source: with cortical inputs terminating on distal dendrites and thalamic inputs terminating perisomatically and on proximal dendrites (Doig et al., 2014; Lapper and Bolam, 1992; Mamaligas et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The higher expression of NaP currents in proximal dendrites preferentially boosts thalamic over cortical inputs.
source: Our finding that the higher expression of NaP currents in proximal dendrites preferentially boosts thalamic over cortical inputs, suggests that active conductances are expressed in CIN dendrites in a manner that corresponds and reinforces the effect of the spatial separation between the terminals of the two inputs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: CIN dendritic excitability is elevated in the Q175 mouse model of HD.
source: As mentioned above, we previously reported that CIN dendritic excitability is elevated in the Q175 mouse model of HD (Tanimura et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: In Q175 mice, cortical EPSCs in CINs are strongly attenuated by ranolazine.
source: In contrast to control (Thy1-ChR2) mice in which cortical EPSPs in CINs are insensitive to ranolazine (Figure 5), cortical EPSCs in CINs from Q175 mice (crossed with Thy1-ChR2 mice) are strongly attenuated by ranolazine.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research and comparison to current study data.

claim: The acquired dependence of distal cortical inputs on NaP currents in Q175 mice results from an upregulation of the NaP current.
source: The acquired dependence of distal cortical inputs on NaP currents in Q175 mice results from an upregulation of the NaP current, which was also evidenced by bAPs invading farther out into the CINs' dendritic arbor (Tanimura et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The elevated excitability in the Q175 mouse is probably a homeostatic response aimed at elevating the postsynaptic sensitivity to the remaining synaptic contents after the loss of afferent cortical and thalamic inputs observed in HD mouse models.
source: This elevated excitability in the Q175 mouse is probably a homeostatic response aimed at elevating the postsynaptic sensitivity to the remaining synaptic contents after the loss of afferent cortical and thalamic inputs observed in HD mouse models (Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: CINs more readily acquired pause responses to cortical inputs in Q175 HD mice than in wildtype mice.
source: Indeed, CINs more readily aquired pause responses to cortical inputs in Q175 HD mice than in wildtype mice (Tanimura et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Thalamostriatal inputs are altered in models of Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Because thalamostriatal inputs are also altered in models of Parkinson's disease (PD) (Aceves Buendia et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2016; Tanimura et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The spatial localization of active dendritic conductances in CIN dendrites corresponds to the spatial distribution of their two main afferent excitatory inputs.
source: In summary, we have used a new optogenetics-based approach, complemented by other electrophysiological and imaging approaches, to demonstrate that the spatial localization of active dendritic conductances that endow CIN dendrites with quasi-linear filtering properties corresponds to the spatial distribution of their two main afferent excitatory inputs.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The matching up of presynaptic terminals with post-synaptic excitability probably contributes to the capacity of CINs to respond differentially to cortical and thalamic inputs.
source: This matching up of presynaptic terminals with post-synaptic excitability, probably contributes to the capacity of CINs to respond differentially to cortical and thalamic inputs.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Sensorimotor information of cortical origin seems to be integrated continuously in a moment-by-moment fashion.
source: Sensorimotor information of cortical origin seems to be integrated continuously in a moment-by-moment fashion.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Thalamic inputs lead to abrupt pauses in TAN firing, even in response to internally generated brain-states (e.g. during slow-wave activity).
source: In contrast, thalamic inputs lead to abrupt pauses in TAN firing, even in response to internally generated brain-states (e.g. during slow-wave activity).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings on TAN responses to slow-wave activity.

claim: The possibility that dendritic arbors adapt to the spatiotemporal patterns of afferent inputs is likely an important principle of neural computation.
source: The possibility that dendritic arbors adapt to the spatiotemporal patterns of afferent inputs is likely an important principle of neural computation that deserves further attention, particularly in the framework of autonomously active neurons such as CINs, SNr neurons and other basal ganglia pacemakers.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation and broader implication of the findings.
